required_facts.statement: A report should be structured for its readers rather than assuming the findings speak for themselves.
source_refs: nngroup_articles#https://www.nngroup.com/articles/engaging-reports-presentations/ — Introduction; Structure Your Report for 3 Audiences

required_facts.statement: Put the key message in headlines for readers who only scan, then provide highlights and supporting detail for readers who need more.
Write at the level of detail the audience needs and select information that serves the report’s purpose.

text.content: Imagine an operations manager receiving a report about dispatch delays. A page of observations alone leaves the reader to find the main conclusion. Structure the report for its readers and purpose.

text.title: Written Business Reports
text.content: A report should be structured for its readers rather than assuming the findings speak for themselves.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Put the key message in headlines for readers who only scan, then provide highlights and supporting detail for readers who need more. Write at the level of detail the audience needs and select information that serves the report’s purpose.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
For this hypothetical report, a headline could state “Instruction clarification is the main issue identified in dispatch preparation.” Highlights then summarize the relevant findings, and supporting detail explains the evidence available in the exercise. The headline is an example report conclusion based on assumed findings, not a claim that clarification is always the main delay.

This layering serves different reading needs. A scanning reader can find the key message; a reader needing more can continue into highlights and detail. Select information that serves the report’s purpose and use the audience’s required level of detail rather than including every note simply because it exists.

The practical output is not a shorter report at any cost. It is an organized report whose key message is prominent and whose supporting information remains available. If the purpose is to communicate the dispatch finding, unrelated observations about office equipment distract from that purpose. Keep enough relevant detail for the intended reader without assuming findings will explain themselves.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Supporting detail does not remove the need for a clear key message. Conversely, a headline alone is not the same as a structured report for readers who need evidence. Use headlines, highlights, and relevant detail rather than choosing between a slogan and an unorganized data dump.

practice_anchor.objective: Write a one-page executive summary for an operations manager from supplied hypothetical raw findings about dispatch delays. Make the key message prominent, organize highlights and supporting detail, and select information relevant to the report's stated purpose.
practice_anchor.success: The submitted summary has a headline supported by the supplied findings, highlights that communicate the relevant findings, and enough supporting detail for the operations manager's stated needs. It excludes unrelated observations, stays within one page, and introduces no unsupported evidence.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show an annotated one-page executive summary for the hypothetical dispatch-delay situation, identifying the key-message headline, highlights, and supporting detail. Make visible how these layers serve scanning readers and readers needing evidence, with a note explaining why an unrelated office-equipment observation is excluded.

notes: Keep example headline explicitly based on hypothetical findings; do not invent evidence.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: The audience determines appropriate detail, terminology, and how information is communicated.
Use the audience’s language and explain an unfamiliar concept with a familiar analogy when useful.
Make the main ideas clear in headlines while preserving supporting detail for readers who need it.

text.content: Suppose the same instruction-access finding must be explained to dispatch managers and to technical colleagues. The audience determines the appropriate detail, terminology, and communication approach.

text.title: Communicating to Technical vs Non-Technical Audiences
text.content: The audience determines appropriate detail, terminology, and how information is communicated.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Use the audience’s language and explain an unfamiliar concept with a familiar analogy when useful. Make the main ideas clear in headlines while preserving supporting detail for readers who need it.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
For managers, a headline might say “Missing instruction matches leave some orders unresolved,” followed by the operational meaning. For technical readers familiar with the query, supporting detail can identify the relevant matching fields and the result behavior. Both explanations should preserve the same finding; changing audience is not permission to change the evidence.

Use the audience’s language. If an unfamiliar relationship needs explanation, a familiar analogy may help: a customer identifier can be compared to a reference that points to a customer record. Use the analogy to clarify the concept, not replace its actual meaning. Keep the main ideas clear in headlines and preserve detail for readers who need it.

The practical skill is selecting how much explanation and which terms serve these readers. A nontechnical audience does not require a different conclusion, and a technical audience does not require every possible implementation detail. The example communications are choices for this hypothetical report, not fixed scripts for everyone with those job titles.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Audience adaptation changes detail and language, not the supported facts. Unexplained jargon can obscure the main idea, while deleting all supporting detail can leave readers unable to understand it. Preserve clear headlines and the detail appropriate to their needs.

practice_anchor.objective: Submit a written rewrite of a supplied technical requirement about instruction access for dispatch managers. Use audience-appropriate language, a clear headline, and supporting detail while preserving the requirement's meaning.
practice_anchor.success: The rewrite preserves the original requirement's conditions and intended behavior without adding unsupported claims. Its headline communicates the main idea, its language suits the stated audience, and necessary supporting detail remains available. Any analogy clarifies rather than replaces the actual meaning.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show technical and non-technical versions of the same instruction-access statement side by side, annotating the shared meaning, audience-specific terminology, clear headline, and retained supporting detail.

notes: Avoid implying all technical or nontechnical audiences have identical knowledge.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: A presentation needs a narrative that makes findings meaningful to its audience rather than a bare list of data.
Structure the presentation around clear headlines, highlights, and supporting detail appropriate to different reader needs.
Use audience-appropriate language and connect findings to the recommendation being communicated.

text.content: Imagine presenting a recommendation about delivery-instruction access. Instead of listing disconnected numbers, build a narrative that makes the findings meaningful to the stakeholder audience.

text.title: Stakeholder Presentations
text.content: A presentation needs a narrative that makes findings meaningful to its audience rather than a bare list of data.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Structure the presentation around clear headlines, highlights, and supporting detail appropriate to different reader needs. Use audience-appropriate language and connect findings to the recommendation being communicated.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
For this hypothetical presentation, the opening headline states the dispatch problem, the next highlight explains the relevant instruction-access finding, and the recommendation follows with its supporting detail. The exact sequence is an example structure, not a compulsory slide count. Use audience-appropriate language to connect the finding to what you recommend.

A reader who scans the headlines should still understand the main ideas. A participant who needs more should be able to follow the highlights and supporting detail. If a chart or table is included, explain its role in the finding rather than assuming the data alone carries the narrative.

The useful output is a presentation whose evidence and recommendation are intelligibly connected for this audience. The hypothetical recommendation must be supported by the assumed findings; do not add persuasive claims merely because they sound compelling. Keep the explanation focused on narrative, layering, language, and connection to the recommendation, not on visual effects or a mandatory presentation template.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: A bare list of data is not necessarily a meaningful presentation. Also, narrative does not mean inventing a more dramatic conclusion. Connect findings to the recommendation with clear headlines, highlights, and appropriate supporting detail for the audience.

practice_anchor.objective: Using a simple slide-outline workspace, outline a five-slide presentation for a specified stakeholder audience from supplied hypothetical findings about delivery-instruction access. Give each slide a clear headline, a key highlight, and appropriate supporting detail, and connect the findings to a supported recommendation.
practice_anchor.success: The five-slide outline forms a meaningful narrative rather than a disconnected list of findings. Its headlines communicate the main ideas in sequence, its highlights and supporting detail serve different reader needs, and its audience-appropriate language connects the supplied evidence to the recommendation without invented claims. Five slides is the exercise constraint, not a general presentation rule.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make a five-slide delivery-instruction presentation outline visible, distinguishing each headline, highlight, and supporting detail. Show how the headlines form a narrative and how the supplied findings support the recommendation.

media.group_title: Connect presentation headlines to supporting evidence

segments.label: Build a narrative with clear headlines and supporting detail
segments.summary: Start with findings and conclusions already established, then organize them into a coherent presentation narrative. The presenter recommends drafting and revising an outline before building slides. Each key statement has supporting evidence beneath it; a homelessness example illustrates this statement-and-evidence structure using different measures over time. Review the argument for audience fit before turning the outline into slide headings and bodies. Headlines should communicate the complete argument when read in sequence, while each slide body should justify its headline. The presenter calls these headlines “action titles” and describes the outline as a “dot-dash” structure. These are ways to connect the main message with the detail that supports it, not requirements to use particular software.

bridge_note.before: Watch how key statements become headlines and evidence becomes supporting detail. The clip calls these “action titles” and “dots and dashes”; its software choices are examples, not requirements.
bridge_note.after: The clip develops narrative and layered evidence, and mentions audience fit. It does not explicitly teach audience-appropriate language; the text covers that requirement and connecting findings to the recommendation.

notes: No unsupported slide counts or persuasive devices.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: Requirements review gives stakeholders and approvers the opportunity to confirm priorities and agree what will be delivered.
Plan a review around the documented goal, scope, requirements, assumptions, and open questions.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Step 4: Document requirements in one shared place

required_facts.statement: Record decisions in the shared requirements document so agreement and unresolved questions remain visible.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Step 4: Document requirements in one shared place

required_facts.statement: Close the walkthrough agenda by asking designated approvers to approve the reviewed requirements or state outstanding conditions, and record the approval outcome, approvers, and any unresolved conditions in the shared decision log.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Step 2: Identify stakeholders and decision-makers; Step 5: Prioritize and validate requirements; What to include in a requirements document — Open questions, Decision log

text.content: Suppose delivery-instruction requirements are ready for stakeholder review. Plan the walkthrough around the documented goal, scope, requirements, assumptions, and open questions. Its purpose is to give stakeholders and approvers an opportunity to confirm priorities and agree what will be delivered.

text.title: Requirements Walkthroughs and Demos
text.content: Requirements review gives stakeholders and approvers the opportunity to confirm priorities and agree what will be delivered.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Plan a review around the documented goal, scope, requirements, assumptions, and open questions. Record decisions in the shared requirements document so agreement and unresolved questions remain visible. Close the walkthrough agenda by asking designated approvers to approve the reviewed requirements or state outstanding conditions, and record the approval outcome, approvers, and any unresolved conditions in the shared decision log.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
In this hypothetical walkthrough, review the instruction-display requirement and its acceptance conditions, then make the unresolved meaning of “current” visible. Record decisions in the shared requirements document instead of letting meeting discussion become the only source of agreement.

Close the agenda by asking designated approvers to approve the reviewed requirements or state outstanding conditions. Record the approval outcome, the approvers, and any unresolved conditions in the shared decision log. For example, the record might state that approval remains conditional on clarifying the instruction-update rule. That is different from recording unconditional approval.

The useful output is a visible agreement and decision record. A demonstration can support discussion, but the fact that a feature was shown does not itself record approval. Keep the reviewed scope and unresolved questions connected to the decision so later readers can understand what was actually agreed and what remains open.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Attendance or a successful demonstration is not an approval record. Ask designated approvers for approval or outstanding conditions, then record the outcome and approvers. Do not rewrite a conditional outcome as full agreement merely because the walkthrough ended.

practice_anchor.objective: Arrange a walkthrough agenda for the delivery-instruction requirements: review the documented goal and scope, examine requirements and assumptions, discuss priorities and open questions, record decisions, and close with an explicit sign-off step for designated approvers.
practice_anchor.success: The agenda covers the documented goal, scope, requirements, assumptions, and open questions; provides for confirming priorities and recording decisions in the shared requirements document; and ends by asking designated approvers for approval or outstanding conditions, with the outcome, approvers, and unresolved conditions recorded in the shared decision log.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the walkthrough agenda sequence visible, ending with designated approvers' approval-or-conditions decision and a shared decision-log entry that distinguishes conditional approval from unconditional approval.

notes: Keep explicit approval closeout; avoid inventing approval authority for the BA.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: A context diagram represents the system as a single element with a boundary separating it from external entities.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/context-diagram — What is a system context diagram?

required_facts.statement: Define the system’s purpose and boundary and identify its external actors and connected systems.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/context-diagram — How to create a system context diagram

required_facts.statement: Draw the system centrally, place external entities around it, and use labeled directional arrows to show exchanges.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/context-diagram — How to create a system context diagram

text.content: Imagine defining the boundary of an order service. A context diagram represents the system as a single central element, with external entities outside its boundary. The immediate question is what is inside this system and what exchanges information with it.

text.title: Scope Modeling / Context Diagrams
text.content: A context diagram represents the system as a single element with a boundary separating it from external entities.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Define the system’s purpose and boundary and identify its external actors and connected systems. Draw the system centrally, place external entities around it, and use labeled directional arrows to show exchanges.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
For this hypothetical diagram, draw “Order service” centrally. Place “Dispatcher” and “External delivery service” around it as external entities. Label directional arrows with the exchanges: a dispatcher sends an order-selection request to the system; the system returns instructions; the system sends a dispatch request to the delivery service. These are example exchanges, not mandatory integrations.

Define the system’s purpose and boundary before placing the entities. Do not put the external delivery service inside merely because it communicates with the order service. The directional labels help the reader distinguish what flows into and out of the central system.

The useful output is a boundary-and-exchange view, not a detailed internal process. The central system stays one element here. That makes the context clear without introducing the internal tasks or screens that may implement it. Read the diagram back as purpose, boundary, external actors or connected systems, and labeled exchanges.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: A context diagram does not expand the system into all its internal activities. It represents the system as one element and shows external entities and exchanges. A connected system is not automatically inside the boundary simply because there is an arrow to it.

practice_anchor.objective: Draw and submit a context diagram for the hypothetical Order service description. State its purpose and boundary, represent it as one central element, place Dispatcher and External delivery service outside it, and add labeled directional arrows for the described exchanges.
practice_anchor.success: The submitted diagram keeps Order service as one central element with a clear boundary. Dispatcher and External delivery service remain outside it. Labeled arrows show an order-selection request from Dispatcher to Order service, instructions from Order service to Dispatcher, and a dispatch request from Order service to External delivery service.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the Order service boundary visible, with one central system element, Dispatcher and External delivery service outside it, and labeled directional arrows distinguishing incoming and outgoing exchanges.

media.group_title: Reading a system boundary and its external exchanges

segments.label: A central system, external connected systems, and information exchanges
segments.summary: The example represents a new portal as one central oval and its connected systems as separate rectangles. These connected systems are external to the portal’s boundary, even when they belong to the same organization. Lines describe information exchanged with the portal: for example, the accounting system sends E-Check information into it. Direction is expressed with pass/pull wording; directional arrows are offered as an alternative. An existing resource center appears without a connection because it is being retired. This is a project-specific scope annotation, not a standard requirement for context diagrams. The explanation places context modeling after understanding the business need and before analyzing detailed requirements, so external connections can be considered early.

bridge_note.before: Watch how the portal stays one central element while connected systems remain separate. The clip calls these “Integrated Systems”; Devspace treats them as external entities relative to the modeled system’s boundary.
bridge_note.after: The clip illustrates the central system and exchanges but does not teach the full purpose, boundary, and external-actor identification procedure. The text supplies those steps and teaches labeled directional arrows.

notes: Avoid internal decomposition and unsupported formal data-flow notation.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: Hierarchical decomposition represents a larger goal as major tasks and breaks those tasks into smaller parts.
Start with the top-level goal, draw its major parts below it, and break each part into relevant subparts.
Choose the number of decomposition levels according to the complexity and detail needed.

text.content: Suppose the top-level goal is “Prepare an order for dispatch.” Functional decomposition represents that larger goal hierarchically through major tasks and smaller parts.

text.title: Functional Decomposition
text.content: Hierarchical decomposition represents a larger goal as major tasks and breaks those tasks into smaller parts.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Start with the top-level goal, draw its major parts below it, and break each part into relevant subparts. Choose the number of decomposition levels according to the complexity and detail needed.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Draw the goal at the top. In this hypothetical decomposition, its major parts are “Identify order,” “Obtain instructions,” and “Prepare dispatch information.” Beneath Obtain instructions, place “Find current instructions” and “Clarify missing information.” These are illustrative parts of the goal, not a universal dispatch procedure.

Choose the number of levels according to the complexity and detail needed. If the analysis only needs the main parts, stop at that useful level. If a part requires more detail for the purpose, break it into relevant subparts. Do not keep adding levels simply to make every branch the same depth.

The useful output is a hierarchy showing how a larger goal breaks into constituent tasks. It is not necessarily execution order: placing two parts side by side shows that they belong under the same parent, not that they occur simultaneously or in a particular sequence. Keep the parent-child meaning explicit so the learner does not confuse this decomposition with the process flows taught earlier.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: A hierarchy of parts is not automatically a sequence of steps. Read lower nodes as subparts of the goal or task above them. The number of levels depends on needed complexity and detail, not an unsupported fixed requirement for every diagram.

practice_anchor.objective: Build a hierarchy for the hypothetical goal “Prepare an order for dispatch,” with two levels of sub-functions beneath it. Place “Identify order,” “Obtain instructions,” and “Prepare dispatch information” at the first level, then add relevant subparts beneath each.
practice_anchor.success: The hierarchy has the given goal at the top, its three major parts directly below it, and relevant smaller parts under each major part. “Find current instructions” and “Clarify missing information” belong beneath “Obtain instructions.” Parent-child links express parts of a function, not execution order; two sub-function levels meet this exercise’s requested detail rather than a universal rule.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the parent-child hierarchy visible: “Prepare an order for dispatch” above its three major parts, with smaller subparts beneath them. Distinguish the two requested sub-function levels without implying execution sequence.

media.group_title: From a business function to its sub-functions

segments.label: Break an order-entry function into major parts and subparts
segments.summary: An order-entry example uses interview notes to identify three major functions: enter customer data, enter product data, and verify price. Customer data entry includes checking credit status and order history. Product data entry includes checking stock status for the product and quantity entered. Price verification includes checking current promotions, quantity discounts, and price updates. These checks form smaller parts beneath their respective parent functions. Functions can be numbered for reference, and the hierarchy can extend to lower levels when more detail is needed.

bridge_note.before: Watch how the order-entry example groups smaller functions beneath major functions. The speaker calls the hierarchy an FDD; here, the emphasis is functional decomposition, not execution order.
bridge_note.after: The clip illustrates major functions, their subparts, and optional deeper levels. Devspace’s text makes explicit that parent-child relationships describe constituent parts, not a required sequence of execution.

notes: Do not infer sequencing from the hierarchy; avoid a mandatory number of levels.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: A spreadsheet formula starts with = and may combine cell references, operators, and functions.
source_refs: excel_support#https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/excel/get-started/overview-of-formulas-in-excel — The parts of an Excel formula

required_facts.statement: A relative reference such as A1 changes when the formula is copied to a different position.
An absolute reference such as $A$1 keeps its row and column fixed when copied; $A1 or A$1 fixes just one part.
Use =SUM(range) to total values, =AVERAGE(range) for their arithmetic mean, and =COUNT(range) to count numeric cells.
Copy a formula containing relative and fixed references and inspect how each reference changes according to the destination.
AVERAGE ignores empty cells and text in a referenced range but includes cells containing zero.

text.content: Imagine a spreadsheet with order amounts in A2:A4 containing 10, 20, and 0, and a factor in B1 containing 0.1. A formula starts with =. To apply the factor to A2, write =A2*$B$1 in C2, then copy it to C3. The relative A2 becomes A3, while the absolute $B$1 stays fixed.

text.title: Cell References and Basic Formulas
text.content: A spreadsheet formula starts with = and may combine cell references, operators, and functions.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: A relative reference such as A1 changes when the formula is copied to a different position. An absolute reference such as $A$1 keeps its row and column fixed when copied; $A1 or A$1 fixes just one part. Use =SUM(range) to total values, =AVERAGE(range) for their arithmetic mean, and =COUNT(range) to count numeric cells. Copy a formula containing relative and fixed references and inspect how each reference changes according to the destination. AVERAGE ignores empty cells and text in a referenced range but includes cells containing zero.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
A relative reference such as A1 changes with the copied position. $A$1 fixes both row and column; $A1 fixes only the column, and A$1 fixes only the row. For example, copying a formula from C2 to D3 shifts a relative A1 to B2, keeps $A$1 unchanged, shifts $A1 to $A2, and shifts A$1 to B$1. Inspect the destination formula instead of assuming every reference moves identically.

For the sample amounts, =SUM(A2:A4) returns 30, =AVERAGE(A2:A4) returns 10, and =COUNT(A2:A4) returns 3 because all three cells are numeric. AVERAGE includes zero. If A4 were empty rather than zero, the average of the referenced numbers would be 15, not 10; text and empty cells are ignored in that range calculation.

The practical skill is reading both the calculation and the reference behavior. Fixed references preserve an intended shared input while relative references move to the corresponding source cell when copied.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: A dollar sign fixes the part it precedes, not always the whole reference. Also, zero and an empty cell do not have the same effect on AVERAGE: zero is included, while empty cells and text in the referenced range are ignored.

practice_anchor.objective: Using order amounts 10, 20, and 0 in A2:A4 and a factor of 0.1 in B1, write a formula in C2 with a relative amount reference and an absolute factor reference, then copy it through C4. Next, fix only the amount column and copy the revised formula across C2:D4.
practice_anchor.success: The first copied formulas use A2, A3, and A4 respectively while retaining $B$1, producing 1, 2, and 0. In the second pass, destination formulas retain column A and $B$1 while the amount row changes: both output columns produce 1, 2, and 0. Inspection confirms the intended references at the bottom-right destination.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the sample amounts and factor alongside source and destination formulas. Make relative row movement, a fully fixed factor, and a column-only fixed amount reference visible during copying down and across. Also show SUM, AVERAGE, and COUNT results, with AVERAGE changing from 10 to 15 when A4 becomes empty or text rather than zero.

media.group_title: Copy formulas with relative, absolute, and mixed references

segments.label: Keep the right references moving or fixed when copying formulas
segments.summary: Relative references preserve their position relative to the formula: copying =C3*2 changes the referenced cell, while =$C$3*2 continues to use C3. A hypothetical clinic example calculates patients served as booked appointments plus walk-ins minus cancellations, then copies calculations across additional days. A sales-bonus example shows why an entirely relative formula can produce incorrect results when copied. Fixing the sales-amount column and the bonus-rate row with separate dollar signs allows one formula to work across rates and down sales rows. Each dollar sign fixes only the part of the reference it precedes.

segments.label: Inspect and correct formulas copied down and across
segments.summary: A hypothetical app-sales spreadsheet uses SUM to calculate annual totals from quarterly values. Copying the formula down changes its range from B5:E5 to B7:E7. A formula beginning with = divides each app’s annual sales by the overall annual total. Copying initially moves both references; fixing the denominator’s row and column keeps the overall total unchanged while the numerator moves. Dollar signs can be entered manually or cycled with F4. A second calculation divides each quarter’s sales by that app’s annual total. Fully fixing $F$5 works across the first row but incorrectly retains that app’s total when copied down. Using $F5 fixes column F while allowing the row to change. Inspecting destination formulas confirms that copying across and down uses the intended cells.

bridge_note.before: Watch how destination formulas reveal which references move. The first clip fixes separate parts; the second corrects an over-fixed reference. Its phrase “column to be free” is a verbal slip: column F stays fixed.
bridge_note.after: The first clip reinforces reference copying; the second also introduces formula entry and SUM. Neither teaches the full SUM/AVERAGE/COUNT set or AVERAGE’s empty/text/zero behavior; the text supplies both.

notes: Trace copying in both directions; no unintroduced conditional or lookup syntax.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: A PivotTable is a tool to calculate, summarize, and analyze data that lets you see comparisons, patterns, and trends in your data.
source_refs: excel_pivottable_guide#Create a PivotTable to analyze worksheet data

required_facts.statement: To create a PivotTable, select the data cells, select Insert > PivotTable, choose where to place the PivotTable report, and select OK.
source_refs: excel_pivottable_guide#Create a PivotTable in Excel for Windows

required_facts.statement: To add a field to the PivotTable, select its checkbox in the PivotTable Fields pane; selected fields are added to their default areas, with non-numeric fields added to Rows and numeric fields added to Values, and a field can be moved to a different area by dragging it there.

Filters area fields are shown as top-level report filters above the PivotTable; Columns area fields are shown as Column Labels at the top of the PivotTable; Rows area fields are shown as Row Labels on the left side of the PivotTable; Values area fields are shown as summarized numeric values in the PivotTable.

text.content: Suppose a worksheet has columns Branch and Amount, with North amounts 40 and 60 and South amount 30. A PivotTable can calculate, summarize, and analyze those rows to reveal comparisons rather than displaying only the original records.

text.title: Pivot Tables
text.content: A PivotTable is a tool to calculate, summarize, and analyze data that lets you see comparisons, patterns, and trends in your data.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: To create a PivotTable, select the data cells, select Insert > PivotTable, choose where to place the PivotTable report, and select OK. To add a field to the PivotTable, select its checkbox in the PivotTable Fields pane; selected fields are added to their default areas, with non-numeric fields added to Rows and numeric fields added to Values, and a field can be moved to a different area by dragging it there. Filters area fields are shown as top-level report filters above the PivotTable; Columns area fields are shown as Column Labels at the top of the PivotTable; Rows area fields are shown as Row Labels on the left side of the PivotTable; Values area fields are shown as summarized numeric values in the PivotTable.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Select the source data cells, choose Insert > PivotTable, select where to place the report, and choose OK. In the PivotTable Fields pane, check Branch and Amount. The nonnumeric Branch field is added to Rows by default, and the numeric Amount field to Values. Fields can be moved by dragging them to the desired area.

Read the areas deliberately. Rows creates row labels on the left, Columns creates column labels at the top, Values displays summarized numeric values, and Filters provides report filters above the PivotTable. In this hypothetical report, using Branch in Rows and Amount summarized by a total in Values gives North 100 and South 30. That illustrates the intended summary; inspect the numeric summary rather than assuming every possible source field produces the same calculation.

The useful output is a summarized view built from field placement. Moving a field changes its role in the report, so explain the placement in business terms: Branch defines the comparison groups and Amount provides the numeric summary.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Checking a field uses its default placement; that placement is not a permanent rule. Drag fields to the area serving the question. Rows, Columns, Filters, and Values are different roles, and a numeric summary should not be mistaken for an original record.

practice_anchor.objective: Using the given Branch and Amount dataset—North 40, North 60, and South 30—build a PivotTable answering: what is the total Amount for each Branch? Select the source cells, create the report in a chosen location, and add Branch and Amount through their field checkboxes. Inspect their placement and move fields if needed.
practice_anchor.success: The PivotTable has Branch in Rows and Amount summarized by a total in Values, showing North 100 and South 30. The learner identifies Branch as the comparison grouping and Amount as the numeric summary.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the Branch and Amount source rows alongside the resulting PivotTable and its Fields pane, making Branch in Rows, Amount in Values, and the North 100 and South 30 totals visible.

media.group_title: Build a PivotTable and choose field roles

segments.label: Create a PivotTable and arrange Rows, Values, Columns, and Filters
segments.summary: Creating a PivotTable begins by selecting source data and choosing Insert > PivotTable. The example also converts the source into a named Excel table before opening the PivotTable dialog, which defaults to a new worksheet. Placing salesperson in Rows and amount in Values produces total sales for each salesperson. Amount is summed because this example's field contains numbers. Geography is then added as a second row grouping and moved to create a column-based comparison. Finally, placing geography in Filters provides a control above the report; selecting New Zealand restricts the displayed sales totals to that geography. Field placement determines how the summary answers the business question.

segments.label: Summarize sales by customer and move Region between Filters and Columns

required_facts.statement: A lookup retrieves a value associated with a matching key.
Use =XLOOKUP(key, lookup_range, return_range) to find a key and return the corresponding value; exact match is the default.
Use =VLOOKUP(key, table_range, column_number, FALSE) for an exact match in the first column and a return value from the specified column to its right.
If VLOOKUP’s final argument is omitted or TRUE, it uses approximate matching and expects the first column sorted.
Use =INDEX(return_range, MATCH(key, lookup_range, 0)) to return the value at the exact key’s position.

text.content: Imagine a customer list with identifiers 101 and 102 in A2:A3 and names North Stores and South Stores in B2:B3. D2 contains the identifier 102. A lookup retrieves the value associated with a matching key.

text.title: Lookup Functions
text.content: A lookup retrieves a value associated with a matching key.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Use =XLOOKUP(key, lookup_range, return_range) to find a key and return the corresponding value; exact match is the default. Use =VLOOKUP(key, table_range, column_number, FALSE) for an exact match in the first column and a return value from the specified column to its right. If VLOOKUP’s final argument is omitted or TRUE, it uses approximate matching and expects the first column sorted. Use =INDEX(return_range, MATCH(key, lookup_range, 0)) to return the value at the exact key’s position.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Write =XLOOKUP(D2,A2:A3,B2:B3) to return South Stores. Exact match is the default. With the same two-column list, =VLOOKUP(D2,A2:B3,2,FALSE) also returns South Stores: it finds an exact key in the first column and returns column 2 to its right.

Do not omit FALSE casually in this exact-key example. If VLOOKUP’s final argument is omitted or TRUE, it uses approximate matching and expects the first column sorted. That is a different lookup mode, not merely shorter spelling for the exact request.

Another exact form is =INDEX(B2:B3,MATCH(D2,A2:A3,0)). MATCH with 0 finds the exact key’s position, and INDEX returns the value at that position from the return range. In the sample, the key is second and the returned name is South Stores.

The useful BA task is joining a needed business label to a known key through the lookup ranges. Keep the ranges aligned in the example so the matching position corresponds to the intended returned value.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: VLOOKUP’s omitted final argument is not exact matching. For the supported exact pattern, use FALSE; approximate matching expects a sorted first column. XLOOKUP’s exact default and MATCH’s 0 also need to be read as part of the chosen lookup form.

practice_anchor.objective: Write a lookup formula that uses the identifier 102 in D2 to retrieve its customer name from a second table, with identifiers 101 and 102 in A2:A3 and names North Stores and South Stores in B2:B3.
practice_anchor.success: The formula returns South Stores using =XLOOKUP(D2,A2:A3,B2:B3), =VLOOKUP(D2,A2:B3,2,FALSE), or =INDEX(B2:B3,MATCH(D2,A2:A3,0)). The chosen formula uses the correct key, source ranges, and exact-match behavior.

required_facts.statement: IF(logical_test, value_if_true, value_if_false) returns one of two results according to the test.
Use =IF(test1, result1, IF(test2, result2, result3)) to express three ordered alternatives.
source_refs: excel_support#https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/excel/functions/if-function — Simple IF examples — discussion of nesting multiple comparisons

required_facts.statement: IFS(test1, result1, test2, result2, ...) returns the result for the first true condition.
A final TRUE condition in IFS supplies a default result; without a true condition, IFS returns #N/A.

text.content: Suppose a spreadsheet labels order amounts using a hypothetical policy: amounts above 100 are High, amounts above 50 but not above 100 are Medium, and the rest are Low. A2 contains the amount to classify.

text.title: Conditional Logic and Formulas
text.content: IF(logical_test, value_if_true, value_if_false) returns one of two results according to the test.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Use =IF(test1, result1, IF(test2, result2, result3)) to express three ordered alternatives. IFS(test1, result1, test2, result2, ...) returns the result for the first true condition. A final TRUE condition in IFS supplies a default result; without a true condition, IFS returns #N/A.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
For a two-way decision, =IF(A2>100,"High","Other") returns High when the test is true and Other when it is false. For three ordered alternatives, use =IF(A2>100,"High",IF(A2>50,"Medium","Low")). The second test is reached only through the false alternative of the first.

The same policy can be written =IFS(A2>100,"High",A2>50,"Medium",TRUE,"Low"). IFS returns the result associated with the first true condition; the final TRUE supplies a default. With amounts 120, 75, and 40, the results are High, Medium, and Low. Exactly 100 is Medium and exactly 50 is Low because these tests use >, not an inclusive comparison.

If the IFS expression contains only the two amount tests and neither is true, it returns #N/A. The final TRUE avoids that no-true-condition case by providing the default. The useful skill is tracing ordered tests rather than assuming the formula evaluates all matching labels and combines them.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: In IFS, the first true condition wins. Putting A2>50 before A2>100 would classify 120 as Medium in this policy. A final TRUE supplies a default; without any true condition, IFS returns #N/A rather than an invented blank or Low label.

practice_anchor.objective: Write a conditional formula using the amount in A2 to implement the hypothetical policy: above 100 is High, above 50 but not above 100 is Medium, and all remaining amounts are Low. Use nested IF or IFS with a final TRUE default.
practice_anchor.success: The formula returns High for 120, Medium for 75 and exactly 100, and Low for 40 and exactly 50. Its ordered tests select the correct branch, and its remaining alternative supplies Low rather than #N/A.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the formula and its result visible alongside the amount in A2 as it changes through 120, 100, 75, 50, and 40, exposing test order, strict threshold boundaries, and the default result.
